claims.text: Tummy time is only for when your baby is awake and an adult is watching closely the whole time.
claims.locator: AAP Back to Sleep: 'The basics of safe sleep & tummy time', item 2; HSE: 'Safety' do-list; AAP safe sleep guide: tummy time section
claims.paraphrase: AAP describes tummy time as for babies who are awake and closely supervised, and says an awake adult should supervise. HSE says always stay with your baby and keep them awake and supervised on their tummy.
claims.scope: All infants; US (AAP) and Ireland (HSE) public guidance agree.

claims.text: If your baby falls asleep during tummy, chest, lap, or carried time, move them onto their back on their own firm, flat sleep surface.
claims.locator: AAP 3 Tummy Time Activities: 'Activity #2: Lap Time'; HSE: 'Safety' don't-list; AAP safe sleep guide: section on babies who fall asleep in car seats, swings, carriers or slings
claims.paraphrase: AAP says a baby who falls asleep on your lap should be transferred to bed on their back; HSE says not to let a baby sleep on their tummy and to roll them onto their back straight away; the AAP safe-sleep guide says babies who fall asleep in a seat, swing, carrier or sling should be moved to a firm sleep surface on their back as soon as possible.
claims.scope: All infants; US and Ireland.

claims.text: Hold your baby on your chest or lap only while you are awake and alert; falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair is especially dangerous.
claims.locator: AAP 3 Tummy Time Activities: 'Activity #1: Tummy to Tummy'; AAP safe sleep guide: 'Share a room with your baby, but never share a bed'
claims.paraphrase: AAP describes chest tummy time while the adult is awake and reclined. The safe-sleep guide says to avoid falling asleep with a baby in other spots, noting a much higher risk of sleep-related death when infants sleep with someone on a couch, soft armchair, or cushion.
claims.scope: All infants; US guidance.

claims.text: For young babies, tummy time can happen on your chest, across your lap, carried tummy-down in your arms, or on a firm mat on the floor.
claims.locator: HSE: 'From birth to 3 months' (chest-to-chest, on your lap, in your arms, on a mat on the floor); AAP: Activities #1 and #2; Children's Wisconsin: 'Why is tummy time important?' position list
claims.paraphrase: HSE lists chest-to-chest, lap, carried face-down in arms, and a firm flat floor mat as tummy-time options from birth to 3 months. AAP describes tummy-to-tummy and lap time. Children's Wisconsin lists tummy to tummy, face to face on the floor, over a small blanket roll, and a tummy carry.
claims.scope: Young infants. Positions differ in whether they count toward a specific target; see the target claims.
claims.caveat: HSE says that from 3 months all tummy time should be on a firm, flat mat.

claims.text: Tummy time helps babies build the neck, shoulder, and back strength they use for rolling, sitting, and crawling.
claims.locator: AAP Back to Sleep: 'Tummy to play'; HSE: opening paragraph; Children's Wisconsin: 'Why is tummy time important?'
claims.paraphrase: All three describe tummy time as building muscles babies need to roll, sit, and crawl; Children's Wisconsin adds back, neck, and shoulder muscles and using eyes and hands together.
claims.scope: General infant guidance; describes purpose, not a guaranteed outcome or timeline.

claims.text: AAP (US): start with short tummy-time sessions of 3–5 minutes, 2–3 times a day, and gradually work up to 15–30 minutes a day by about 7 weeks as your baby enjoys it.
claims.locator: Section 'How much tummy time should a baby have?'
claims.paraphrase: Play with your awake baby on their tummy two to three times a day for three to five minutes, starting from the day you come home, and build up to 15–30 minutes a day by 7 weeks.
claims.scope: US general guidance for infants. The same page lists chest play among tummy-time ideas and does not say that only floor time counts toward the daily amount.

claims.text: Children's Wisconsin (US): start with 2–3 minutes at a time and slowly work up to a total of at least 60 minutes a day by the time your baby is 4 months old.
claims.locator: Section 'Why is tummy time important?' — 'How can I make tummy time happy?'
claims.paraphrase: Supervise tummy time when awake, start on the first day, keep it happy, begin with 2–3 minutes, and work up to at least 60 minutes per day total by 4 months.
claims.scope: One US children's hospital's teaching sheet. Its suggested positions include tummy-to-tummy on your chest, face to face on the floor, over a small blanket roll, and a tummy carry; it does not say that only floor time counts.
claims.caveat: Higher than the AAP page's 15–30 minutes by 7 weeks; the two cover different ages and come from different organizations.

claims.text: HSE (Ireland): aim for at least 30 minutes a day, spread out, in the first 3 months, then build up to 60 minutes between 4 and 6 months. From 3 months, all tummy time should be on a firm, flat mat.
claims.locator: Sections 'When to start' and 'From 3 months'
claims.paraphrase: Begin with 2–3 minutes a few times a day, aim for at least 30 minutes a day in the first 3 months, build to 60 minutes between 4 and 6 months; chest, lap, arms and floor-mat positions are described for birth to 3 months, and from 3 months all tummy time should be on a firm, flat mat.
claims.scope: Ireland public health guidance for infants generally.
claims.caveat: Position rule is HSE's; US sources quoted here do not restrict positions the same way.

claims.text: SickKids neonatal follow-up (Canada): at 4 months corrected age, 50–60 minutes of tummy time a day in short periods, with as much floor play as possible.
claims.locator: 'Neonatal follow-up clinic recommendations at four months' — 'Gross motor' list
claims.paraphrase: Practice floor time for play as much as possible (the bed is not a safe place to play); practice tummy time, between 50 and 60 minutes total per day in short periods, to improve head and trunk control.
claims.scope: Babies followed by a neonatal follow-up clinic, mostly after NICU or cardiac critical care; ages are corrected age. The page says to ask your child's doctor whether to follow it.
claims.caveat: The page emphasizes floor play but does not list which positions count toward the 50–60 minutes.

claims.text: WHO (global, 2019): babies who are not yet mobile should have at least 30 minutes a day on their tummy while awake, spread through the day, as part of interactive floor-based play.
claims.locator: 'Recommendations at a glance' — Infants (less than 1 year), first bullet
claims.paraphrase: Infants should be physically active several times a day, particularly through interactive floor-based play; for those not yet mobile this includes at least 30 minutes in prone position spread through the day while awake.
claims.scope: International guidance for infants under 1 year who are not yet mobile.

claims.text: Changing your awake baby's position and limiting long stretches in car seats, swings, and bouncy seats reduces pressure on the back of the head.
claims.locator: AAP: 'There are ways to reduce the risk of the baby developing a flat spot'; Children's Wisconsin: 'How do I keep my baby from getting a flat head and tight neck muscles?'
claims.paraphrase: Vary the awake baby's position, hold them, and watch them play on tummy and back on the floor; limit time in swings, bouncy chairs, and car seats, which press on the back of the head.
claims.scope: Young infants; general guidance, not treatment for an existing head-shape concern.

claims.text: Use a firm, flat surface on the floor for floor play and tummy time, not a bed, sofa, or cushion.
claims.locator: SickKids: 'Gross motor', first bullet; HSE: 'On a mat on the floor' and 'From 3 months'; AAP 3 Tummy Time Activities: 'More tummy-time tips' (secure blankets)
claims.paraphrase: SickKids says the bed is not an appropriate or safe place to play and the floor is a safer, firmer surface. HSE describes a firm, flat mat on the floor. AAP suggests a clean floor, mat, or blankets secured so they don't slide.
claims.scope: Infants; Canada, Ireland, and US sources agree on a firm floor surface.

claims.text: On their tummy, a toy placed in front of or just beside your baby encourages them to lift their head, turn, shift their weight, and reach.
claims.locator: HSE: 'From 3 months'; AAP: 'How can I exercise my baby during tummy time?'
claims.paraphrase: HSE suggests a toy in front to encourage head lifting, then encouraging turning, balancing on one arm to reach, and moving forward as the baby gets stronger. AAP suggests a toy or yourself just out of reach and toys in a circle around the baby.
claims.scope: Infants playing on their tummy; HSE frames this from 3 months.

claims.text: While an adult keeps watch, a young child can get down on the floor and play with a baby during tummy time.
claims.locator: Section 'How can I exercise my baby during tummy time?', last bullet
claims.paraphrase: While keeping watch, have a young child play with the baby on their tummy; young children get on the floor easily, have energy for playing with babies, and may enjoy the 'big kid' role.
claims.scope: US general guidance. The adult supervises; the child is a playmate, not a caregiver.

claims.text: Keep tummy time short and happy: stop when your baby becomes upset and try again later, building up gradually as they enjoy it.
claims.locator: HSE: 'Safety' do-list; AAP: 'How much tummy time…'; Children's Wisconsin: 'How can I make tummy time happy?'
claims.paraphrase: HSE says stop and try again later if the baby becomes upset. AAP says increase gradually as babies show they enjoy it. Children's Wisconsin says time on the tummy should be happy.
claims.scope: All infants; US and Ireland.

claims.text: HSE (Ireland) suggests avoiding tummy time just before or after a feed, especially if your baby has reflux.
claims.locator: Section 'When to start', last paragraph
claims.paraphrase: Avoid tummy time just before or after a feed, especially if your baby has reflux.
claims.scope: Ireland public guidance; a practical timing tip, not a feeding schedule.

claims.text: If your baby was born early, has reflux, or has other medical needs, ask their clinician about tummy time; many follow-up teams use corrected age.
claims.locator: AAP: 'Tummy time & babies with special health care needs'; SickKids: 'What is the Neonatal Follow-Up Clinic?' (corrected age)
claims.paraphrase: AAP says to speak with your pediatrician about tummy time if your baby was premature or has reflux or special needs. SickKids notes its recommendations are for corrected age because most babies it follows were premature.
claims.scope: Babies with prematurity or medical needs; US and Canada.

claims.text: When young children are sitting still, interactive non-screen time with a caregiver—reading, storytelling, singing, puzzles—is encouraged.
claims.locator: Body paragraph on 24-hour activity patterns; 'Recommendations at a glance' bullets for each age group
claims.paraphrase: Quality sedentary time in interactive non-screen activities with a caregiver, such as reading, storytelling, singing, and puzzles, is very important for development; when sedentary, reading and storytelling with a caregiver is encouraged.
claims.scope: International guidance for children under 5.

claims.text: WHO (global): children under 5 shouldn't be kept restrained—in a stroller, high chair, or carrier—for more than an hour at a time.
claims.locator: 'Recommendations at a glance', second bullet for each age group
claims.paraphrase: Infants, 1–2-year-olds, and 3–4-year-olds should not be restrained for more than 1 hour at a time (e.g., prams/strollers, high chairs, strapped on a caregiver's back).
claims.scope: International guidance for children under 5.

claims.text: WHO (global): babies benefit from active, floor-based play several times a day; children 1–4 benefit from at least 180 minutes of varied physical activity spread through the day.
claims.locator: 'Recommendations at a glance', first bullet for each age group
claims.paraphrase: Infants should be active several times a day, particularly through interactive floor-based play. Children 1–2 and 3–4 should spend at least 180 minutes in a variety of physical activities spread through the day; for 3–4-year-olds at least 60 of those minutes are moderate-to-vigorous.
claims.scope: International guidance; daily totals across the whole day, not per activity.

claims.text: WHO (global, 2019): no sedentary screen time for babies or 1-year-olds; for ages 2–4, no more than 1 hour a day, and less is better.
claims.locator: 'Recommendations at a glance', second bullet for each age group
claims.paraphrase: Screen time is not recommended for infants; for 1-year-olds sedentary screen time is not recommended; for 2-year-olds and 3–4-year-olds no more than 1 hour, less is better.
claims.scope: International guidance (2019).
claims.caveat: Stricter for 1-year-olds than the current AAP explainer, which emphasizes quality, context, and co-viewing over fixed limits.

claims.text: AAP (US, 2026): babies under 18 months learn best from real-world interactions, and heavy solo screen use can affect young children's language and social skills.
claims.locator: Section 'Early childhood (0-5 years)'
claims.paraphrase: Infants under 18 months learn best from real-world interactions; heavy solo screen use can affect developing language and social skills, with outcomes depending on hours of use and how adults use screens to calm or entertain.
claims.scope: US; children 0–5, with the real-world-learning statement specific to under 18 months.

claims.text: AAP (US, 2026): choose quality content that puts kids first, watch alongside your child when you can, and keep screen-free times such as meals and the hour before bed.
claims.locator: Section 'Tips for helping your child navigate the digital ecosystem'
claims.paraphrase: Seek out quality content that models social-emotional skills or fosters play; watch and play alongside your kids; carve out screen-free time and zones such as mealtimes and the hour before bed; use a family media plan.
claims.scope: US family guidance across ages; frames media around quality, context, and conversation rather than a single time limit.

activities.title: Chest-to-chest tummy time
activities.summary: Recline, awake and supported, with your baby tummy-down on your chest, and chat face to face.

notes: Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about tummy time first.

supervision.space: Reclined in a chair, on a bed, or on the floor with your head supported—only while you're wide awake.

steps: Recline with your head and back supported so you can see your baby's face.
Lay your baby tummy-down on your chest, one hand resting on their back.
Talk, smile, and make big expressions so they lift their head to look at you.
As they get stronger over the weeks, recline a little flatter.
adaptations: Very new baby: a minute or two is plenty; let them rest their cheek on you between tries.
Stronger baby: lie flatter so lifting their head takes more work.
stopCues: Getting drowsy—move them to their back in their own sleep space

safety.text: Only while you're awake and alert. If you feel sleepy, put your baby on their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Lifting their head to see your face is tummy time: it builds the neck and shoulder strength babies use for rolling and sitting.

activities.title: Lap tummy time
activities.summary: Lay your baby tummy-down along your lap, support their head, and gently sway your knees while you talk.

notes: Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about tummy time first.

supervision.space: Seated securely with both feet down, one hand always on your baby.

steps: Sit with your knees together and lay your baby tummy-down along your thighs.
Keep their head in line with their body, supporting it with your hand as needed.
Stroke their back, talk softly, or sway your knees slowly from side to side.
adaptations: Turn them so they can see a window, a face, or a high-contrast picture.
Calmer baby: slow, rhythmic back pats; alert baby: chat and pause for their sounds.

safety.text: Keep a hand on your baby. If they fall asleep, move them onto their back in their own sleep space.

why.text: Lap time is one of the tummy-time positions suggested for young babies who are still getting used to being on their tummy.

activities.title: Face-to-face floor tummy time
activities.summary: Put your baby tummy-down on a firm, flat mat on the floor and lie down at their eye level to chat.

notes: Born early, reflux, or medical needs? Ask your baby's clinician about tummy time first.

items: Firm play mat or a blanket on a clean floor

supervision.space: Firm, flat floor surface—never a bed, sofa, or cushion. Smooth the blanket so it can't bunch.

steps: Lay a firm mat or smoothed blanket on a clear patch of floor.
Place your baby tummy-down with their elbows tucked under their shoulders.
Lie down face to face and talk, sing, or hold a toy at their eye level.
Roll them onto their back for a rest when they've had enough.
adaptations: Short and often beats long: 1–3 minutes a few times a day is a fine start.
Add a high-contrast card or your face just in front to give them something to lift up for.

safety.text: Only while awake, with you right there. If they get sleepy, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
Use the floor, not a bed or sofa.

why.text: Short, frequent tummy sessions on the floor help babies build the strength they'll use to roll, sit, and crawl.

activities.title: Tummy time reach and play
activities.summary: On a firm floor mat, place a toy just ahead or to one side so your baby lifts up, turns, and reaches.

notes: Your baby sets the pace; short, happy sessions count. Ask their clinician if they were born early.

items: 1–3 baby-safe toys or an unbreakable mirror

supervision.space: Firm, flat floor surface with a clear area around the mat; stay within arm's reach.

steps: Lay your baby tummy-down on a firm, flat mat on the floor.
Hold a toy or unbreakable mirror just in front, then move it slowly side to side.
Set it down a little to one side so they shift onto one arm to reach.
Let them get it before they get frustrated, then cheer their effort.
adaptations: Just starting out: keep the toy close and at eye level.
Pushing up on straight arms: place toys in a loose circle so they pivot to reach.

safety.text: Only while awake and watched. If they fall asleep, move them to their back in their own sleep space.
Firm floor only; toys must be too big to fit in your baby's mouth.

why.text: Reaching for a toy on their tummy asks babies to lift, turn, and shift weight, building strength for rolling and crawling.
